claim: One hour of hormone exposure was sufficient to induce 29934 GR binding sites/peaks identified specifically in Dex-treated cells.
source: One hour of hormone exposure was sufficient to induce a massive DNA binding response by GR, with 29934 GR binding sites/peaks identified specifically in Dex-treated cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data showing GR binding sites after Dex treatment, as stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of GR peaks called from this dataset falls within the range of peak numbers called by GR ChIP-seq experiments in other cell lines.
source: The number of peaks called from our dataset falls within the range of peak numbers called by GR ChIP-seq experiments in other cell lines (Swinstead et al., 2016; Starick et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published studies cited in the text.

claim: Dex treatment had a robust effect on the chromatin localization of BRG1.
source: Dex treatment also had a robust effect on the chromatin localization of BRG1.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing changes in BRG1 binding patterns upon Dex treatment.

claim: While 50,000+ BRG1 peaks were identified in each condition, only 33582 peaks were shared while 17699 were specific to EtOH-treated cells and 20658 were specific to Dex-treated cells.
source: While 50,000 + BRG1 peaks were identified in each condition, only 33582 peaks were shared while 17699 were specific to EtOH-treated cells and 20658 were specific to Dex-treated cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data analysis showing peak overlap between conditions, as presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: This rearrangement of BRG1 chromatin localization is consistent with BRG1 being recruited to GBSs upon hormone treatment.
source: This rearrangement of BRG1 chromatin localization is consistent with BRG1 being recruited to GBSs upon hormone treatment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed BRG1 redistribution data.

claim: 58% of GR peaks are overlapped by a BRG1 peak.
source: To verify this, we examined the overlap between BRG1 and GR peaks and found that 58% of GR peaks are overlapped by a BRG1 peak (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq peaks shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: There was significant overlap in both EtOH and Dex-treated cells, with 12034 GR peaks bound by BRG1 in both conditions, and 5565 bound by BRG1 in a Dex-specific manner.
source: Surprisingly, there was significant overlap in both EtOH and Dex-treated cells (Figure 1B), with 12034 GR peaks bound by BRG1 in both conditions, and 5565 bound by BRG1 in a Dex-specific manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative overlap analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: 12223 GR peaks were not bound by BRG1.
source: 12223 GR peaks were not bound by BRG1, and a total of 54340 BRG1 peaks (including 15093 Dex-specific and 17699 EtOH-specific) did not overlap GR (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A large subset of the subsequent GR peaks are bound by BRG1 prior to hormone treatment consistent with the concept that BRG1 could be involved in pre-patterning GBSs.
source: These findings indicate that a large subset of the subsequent GR peaks are bound by BRG1 prior to hormone treatment consistent with the concept that BRG1 could be involved in pre-patterning GBSs.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed BRG1 binding patterns prior to hormone treatment.

claim: Class I GR peaks were narrower and showed less overall GR enrichment than Class II or Class III peaks.
source: Collectively, Class I GR peaks were narrower and showed less overall GR enrichment than Class II or Class III peaks (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: BRG1 was not enriched at Class I GR peaks, was constitutively enriched at Class II GR peaks, and was induced by Dex-treatment at Class III peaks.
source: BRG1 was not enriched at Class I GR peaks, was constitutively enriched at Class II GR peaks, and was induced by Dex-treatment at Class III peaks (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1E,G.

claim: Short, sub-nucleosome length ATAC-seq reads were strongly enriched at Class II peaks independent of Dex treatment.
source: Short, sub-nucleosome length ATAC-seq reads were used as a measure of chromatin accessibility, and were strongly enriched at Class II peaks independent of Dex treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: Class II GR peaks are accessible prior to hormone treatment.
source: Thus, Class II GR peaks are accessible prior to hormone treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Minimal accessibility was detected at Class I and III GR peaks in EtOH-treated cells, indicating that prior to hormone treatment, these GR peaks were largely inaccessible.
source: Conversely, minimal accessibility was detected at Class I and III GR peaks in EtOH-treated cells, indicating that prior to hormone treatment, these GR peaks were largely inaccessible (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon 1 hr Dex exposure, low but distinct levels of accessibility were induced, predominantly at class III peaks where BRG1 binding was also induced.
source: Upon 1 hr Dex exposure, low but distinct levels of accessibility were induced, predominantly at class III peaks where BRG1 binding was also induced (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Chromatin accessibility at GR peak classes was directly correlated with the pattern of BRG1 occupancy.
source: Thus, chromatin accessibility at GR peak classes was directly correlated with the pattern of BRG1 occupancy.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the correlation between ATAC-seq and BRG1 ChIP-seq data.

claim: H3K27ac ChIP-seq coverage is specifically enriched over Class II GR peaks independently of hormone treatment.
source: Histone 3 Lysine 27 acetylation (K27ac), a histone modification associated with transcriptionally active chromatin at TSSs and active enhancers, was only detected at Class II GR peaks (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: H3K4me1 was enriched at all three peaks classes, but had a unique pattern at Class II peaks.
source: Histone 3 Lysine four monomethylation (K4me1), a marker of both inactive/poised and active enhancers, was enriched at all three peaks classes, but had a unique pattern at Class II peaks (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by H3K4me1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: While K4me1 enrichment was centered on the GR peak at Class I and III peaks, Class II peaks had broader K4me1 enrichment with an apparent trough of enrichment directly over the GR peak.
source: While K4me1 enrichment was centered on the GR peak at Class I and III peaks, Class II peaks had broader K4me1 enrichment with an apparent trough of enrichment directly over the GR peak (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by H3K4me1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: None of the peak Classes displayed strong enrichment of H3K27me3, a repressive chromatin modification.
source: None of the peak Classes displayed strong enrichment of Histone 3 Lysine 27 trimethylation (K27me3), a repressive chromatin modification (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The patterns of histone modifications at GR peaks were associated with enhancer-like chromatin marks.
source: Taken together with the ATAC-seq data, the patterns of histone modifications at GR peaks were associated with enhancer-like chromatin marks.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined analysis of ATAC-seq and histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: The strong ATAC accessibility signal and K27ac enrichment at Class II peaks suggested that they might represent GR binding to active enhancers.
source: The strong ATAC accessibility signal and K27ac enrichment at Class II peaks suggested that they might represent GR binding to active enhancers.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on ATAC-seq and H3K27ac ChIP-seq data.

claim: The relatively low levels of ATAC accessibility and the patterns of K4me1 and K27ac at Class I and III peaks suggested that they represented GR binding to inactive or poised enhancers.
source: On the other hand, the relatively low levels of ATAC accessibility and the patterns of K4me1 and K27ac at Class I and III peaks suggested that they represented GR binding to inactive or poised enhancers.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on ATAC-seq and histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: Class II GR peaks represent a distinct set of GR peaks that are associated with BRG1 as well as marks of accessible and transcriptionally active chromatin.
source: Furthermore, Class II GR peaks represent a distinct set of GR peaks that are associated with BRG1 as well as marks of accessible and transcriptionally active chromatin.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined analysis of BRG1 ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and histone modification data.

claim: GR ChIP-seq signal after 1 hr of Dex treatment was modestly enriched over active gene TSSs.
source: GR ChIP-seq signal after 1 hr of Dex treatment was modestly enriched over active gene TSSs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), however this was dwarfed by the level of GR enrichment at active enhancer TSSs identified in either EtOH- and Dex-treated cells (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by GR ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2E–G.

claim: GR was much more frequently associated with enhancer transcription than gene transcription.
source: Thus, GR was much more frequently associated with enhancer transcription than gene transcription.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the comparison of GR enrichment at gene TSSs versus enhancer TSSs.

claim: BRG1 ChIP-seq signal was broadly detected and similarly enriched at all active TSSs.
source: Unlike GR, BRG1 ChIP-seq signal was broadly detected and similarly enriched at all active TSSs (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Over active gene TSSs and EtOH-detected active enhancers, the average levels BRG1 enrichment appeared unaffected by Dex.
source: Over active gene TSSs and EtOH-detected active enhancers, the average levels BRG1 enrichment appeared unaffected by Dex (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: BRG1 was largely associated with open and active chromatin independently of GR.
source: Taken together, these data indicated that BRG1 was largely associated with open and active chromatin independently of GR, and that BRG1 peaks that were not affected by hormone treatment most strongly exhibited these characteristics.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined analysis of BRG1 ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and histone modification data.

claim: A Dex-induced increase in BRG1 enrichment was observed at active enhancer TSSs detected in Dex-treated cells.
source: However, a Dex-induced increase in BRG1 enrichment was observed at active enhancer TSSs detected in Dex-treated cells (Figure 2G), and more modestly at the TSSs of Dex-induced DEGs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: TSSs with altered transcriptional activity upon Dex exposure also exhibited hormone-induced BRG1 enrichment.
source: Thus, TSSs with altered transcriptional activity upon Dex exposure also exhibited hormone-induced BRG1 enrichment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the correlation between transcriptional activity changes and BRG1 enrichment.

claim: When considering active TSSs called in untreated cells, 38% of Class II peaks were within 1 kb of a TSS, compared to 2% of Class I peaks and 7% of Class III peaks.
source: When considering active TSSs called in untreated cells, 38% of Class II peaks were within 1 kb of a TSS, compared to 2% of Class I peaks and 7% of Class III peaks (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by distance analysis between GR peaks and TSSs shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When considering active TSSs called in cells treated with Dex for 1 hr, a significant portion of each peak class was within 1 kb of a TSS (26% Class I, 45% Class II, and 38% Class III).
source: However, when considering active TSSs called in cells treated with Dex for 1 hr, a significant portion of each peak class was within 1 kb of a TSS (26% Class I, 45% Class II, and 38% Class III) (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by distance analysis between GR peaks and TSSs shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Class II peaks represented GR interactions with accessible chromatin and transcriptionally active enhancers.
source: Taken together with the patterns of K27ac and K4me1, these data indicated that Class II peaks represented GR interactions with accessible chromatin and transcriptionally active enhancers.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined analysis of chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and TSS proximity data.

claim: Class I and III peaks represented GR interactions with inactive or poised enhancers that could be activated upon GR binding, but exhibited limited accessibility and were devoid of the K27ac mark.
source: Furthermore, they indicated that Class I and III peaks represented GR interactions with inactive or poised enhancers that could be activated upon GR binding, but exhibited limited accessibility and were devoid of the K27ac mark.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined analysis of chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and TSS proximity data.

claim: Treatment with Doxycycline for 72 hr resulted in an 80–85% reduction in BRG1 protein levels as well as partial reduction in the nuclear levels of GR protein.
source: Treatment with Doxycycline for 72 hr resulted in an 80–85% reduction in BRG1 protein levels as well as partial reduction in the nuclear levels of GR protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In normal conditions, 1244 DEGs (Fold Change > 1.5, p-value<0.01, false discovery rate <0.05) were identified following 8 hr of Dex treatment.
source: In normal conditions, 1244 DEGs (Fold Change > 1.5, p-value<0.01, false discovery rate <0.05) were identified following 8 hr of Dex treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 743 of these DEGs failed to meet the same fold-change and significance cutoffs in Dex treated BRG1-KD cells, indicating BRG1 was required the transcriptional response to Dex.
source: 743 of these DEGs failed to meet the same fold-change and significance cutoffs in Dex treated BRG1-KD cells, indicating BRG1 was required the transcriptional response to Dex.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing wild-type and BRG1-KD cells.

claim: BRG1-KD cells had 114 Dex-regulated DEGs that were not called DEGs in control Dex-treated cells, indicating that BRG1 also suppressed the hormone responsiveness of a small number of genes.
source: Intriguingly, BRG1-KD cells had 114 Dex-regulated DEGs that were not called DEGs in control Dex-treated cells, indicating that BRG1 also suppressed the hormone responsiveness of a small number of genes (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing wild-type and BRG1-KD cells shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The absolute fold change of both 'common' and 'lost' DEGs was reduced in BRG1-KD cells, and increased in 'gained' DEGs.
source: Indeed, the absolute fold change of both 'common' and 'lost' DEGs was reduced in BRG1-KD cells, and increased in 'gained' DEGs (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BRG1 was required for both a robust transcription hormone response and to suppress ectopic hormone responsiveness.
source: Together, these data indicated that BRG1 was required for both a robust transcription hormone response and to suppress ectopic hormone responsiveness.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the RNA-seq data comparing wild-type and BRG1-KD cells.

claim: Reduction of GR protein levels by 50–70% by siRNA resulted in a modest loss of dex-induced transcription at candidate 'lost' genes.
source: Reduction of GR protein levels by 50–70% by siRNA resulted in a modest loss of dex-induced transcription at candidate 'lost' genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: BRG1-KD resulted in a much stronger loss of dex-induced transcription than GR siRNA.
source: However, BRG1-KD resulted in a much stronger loss of dex-induced transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The changes in the Dex response in A1A3 cells are predominantly driven by the silencing of BRG1, and not by the more modest decrease in nuclear GR levels.
source: As such, these data strongly suggest that the changes in the Dex response in A1A3 cells are predominantly driven by the silencing of BRG1, and not by the more modest decrease in nuclear GR levels.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the comparison of GR siRNA and BRG1-KD effects on gene expression.

claim: DEG TSSs tended to be closer to GR peaks, and the percentage of DEGs with GR peaks within 50 kb was more than double that of non-DEG obsTSSs (77.2 to 29.8%).
source: DEG TSSs tended to be closer to GR peaks, and the percentage of DEGs with GR peaks within 50 kb was more than double that of non-DEG obsTSSs (77.2 to 29.8%).
evidence: The claim is supported by distance analysis between DEG TSSs and GR peaks.

claim: While GR binding is distal from gene TSSs, genes that are regulated by GR tend to have a higher degree of local GR binding sites.
source: Thus, while GR binding is distal from gene TSSs, genes that are regulated by GR tend to have a higher degree of local GR binding sites.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the distance analysis between DEG TSSs and GR peaks.

claim: When considering the closest GR peak to each DEG, the different types of DEGs had different proportions of GR peaks classes, with Class II peaks enriched among the closest peaks to 'common' and 'gained' DEGs.
source: When considering the closest GR peak to each DEG, the different types of DEGs had different proportions of GR peaks classes, with Class II peaks enriched among the closest peaks to 'common' and 'gained' DEGs (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of GR peak classes near DEGs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Class II peaks were closer to DEG TSSs than Class I or Class III peaks.
source: Comparing the distance from the closest GR peak to each DEG TSS, Class II peaks were also closer than Class I or Class III peaks (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 'Common' DEGs had closer GR peaks than 'gained' or 'lost' DEGs, with the median distance from TSSs to closest GR peaks of 6889, 20094, and 22104 bp, respectively.
source: Overall, 'common' DEGs had closer GR peaks than 'gained' or 'lost' DEGs, with the median distance from TSSs to closest GR peaks of 6889, 20094, and 22104 bp, respectively (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: DEGs that were 'gained' or 'lost' also had fewer GR peaks within 50 kb of their TSSs.
source: DEGs that were 'gained' or 'lost' also had fewer GR peaks within 50 kb of their TSSs (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: BRG1 presence was more critical for hormone responsiveness at genes where GR binding was the most distal.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that BRG1 presence was more critical for hormone responsiveness at genes where GR binding was the most distal.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the correlation between GR peak distance and BRG1 requirement for gene regulation.

claim: Using the total set of GR peaks, perfect GREs were found under 28.3% of the peaks and GREs with single mismatches were found under an additional 51% of peaks.
source: Using the total set of GR peaks, perfect GREs were found under 28.3% of the peaks and GREs with single mismatches were found under an additional 51% of peaks (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Perfect GREs were more common in Class I and Class III peaks (33 and 35.3%, respectively) than Class II peaks (19.4%).
source: Perfect GREs were more common in Class I and Class III peaks (33 and 35.3%, respectively) than Class II peaks (19.4%) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GREs, Androgen Receptor motifs, and Progesterone Receptor motifs were strongly enriched under all three peak classes, but with the lowest enrichment levels under Class II peaks.
source: Motif analysis revealed similar patterns, with GREs, Androgen Receptor motifs, and Progesterone Receptor motifs being strongly enriched under all three peak classes, but with the lowest enrichment levels under Class II peaks (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Class II peaks exhibited the highest average level of motif enrichment.
source: Motif analysis revealed that Class II peaks exhibited the highest average level of motif enrichment (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FOX and GATA motifs were more strongly enriched under Class II peaks than Class I or Class III peaks.
source: This was largely driven by FOX and GATA motifs, which were more strongly enriched under Class II peaks than Class I or Class III peaks (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Class II GR peaks displayed the strongest levels of enrichment for ENCODE transcription factor ChIP-seq signal, while Class I and Class III peaks showed only low to moderate levels of enrichment.
source: Class II GR peaks displayed the strongest levels of enrichment, while Class I and Class III peaks showed only low to moderate levels of enrichment (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ENCODE transcription factor ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SP/KLF and POU motifs were specifically enriched under Class II and Class III peaks.
source: SP/KLF and POU motifs were specifically enriched under Class II and Class III peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which suggested that GR binding in cooperation with these transcription factor families may also involve BRG1.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: STAT, NFATC, and OLIG motifs were most strongly enriched under Class I GR peaks.
source: On the other hand, STAT, NFATC, and OLIG motifs were most strongly enriched under Class I GR peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicative of transcription factor interactions that may occur in the absence of BRG1.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The three GR peak classes had distinguishable DNA sequence content and the BRG1-GR interaction could be moderated by other transcription factors.
source: Taken together, these analyses revealed that the three GR peak classes had distinguishable DNA sequence content and that the BRG1-GR interaction could be moderated by other transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the motif analysis and transcription factor ChIP-seq data.

claim: Both FOXA1 and GATA3 showed strong levels of enrichment at Class II GR peaks in both untreated and 1 hr Dex treated cells.
source: Both FOXA1 and GATA3 showed strong levels of enrichment at Class II GR peaks in both untreated and 1 hr Dex treated cells (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Class I and Class III peaks had similarly low levels of FOXA1 and GATA3 in untreated cells.
source: Class I and Class III peaks had similarly low levels of FOXA1 and GATA3 in untreated cells (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: At Class III peaks, there was a marked increase in the detected levels of FOXA1 and GATA3 binding upon 1 hr of Dex treatment.
source: However, at Class III peaks, there was a marked increase in the detected levels of FOXA1 and GATA3 binding upon 1 hr of Dex treatment (Figure 5A–B) comparable to the Dex-induced enrichment of BRG1 at these peaks (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: At GR peaks, the pattern of pioneer factor binding correlated with that of BRG1 binding.
source: Thus, at GR peaks, the pattern of pioneer factor binding correlated with that of BRG1 binding.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the correlation between FOXA1/GATA3 and BRG1 ChIP-seq patterns.

claim: The levels of FOXA1 and GATA3 protein were similar between control and BRG1-KD cells, indicating that BRG1 was not required for their expression.
source: The levels of FOXA1 and GATA3 protein were similar between control and BRG1-KD cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that BRG1 was not required for their expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In control cells treated with Dex for 1 hr, a Dex-induced increase in FOXA1 and GATA3 enrichment was observed at all three GR peak classes, with the most substantial increase occurring at Class III peaks.
source: In control cells treated with Dex for 1 hr, a Dex-induced increase in FOXA1 and GATA3 enrichment was observed at all three GR peak classes, with the most substantial increase occurring at Class III peaks (Figure 5C–D, left columns)).
evidence: The claim is supported by FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data in A1A3 cells shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: In vehicle treated BRG1-KD cells, the loss of BRG1 appeared to have little effect on the enrichment of FOXA1 and GATA3 at GR peaks.
source: In vehicle treated BRG1-KD cells, the loss of BRG1 appeared to have little effect on the enrichment of FOXA1 and GATA3 at GR peaks (Figure 5C–D, red lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data in BRG1-KD cells shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: The DEX-induced increase in FOXA1 and GATA3 enrichment at GR peaks was almost completely blocked in BRG1-KD cells.
source: In contrast, the DEX-induced increase in FOXA1 and GATA3 enrichment at GR peaks was almost completely blocked in BRG1-KD cells (Figure 5C–D, blue lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data in BRG1-KD cells shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: BRG1 was not required for pioneer factor interaction at GR peaks.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that BRG1 was not required for pioneer factor interaction at GR peaks.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data in BRG1-KD cells.

claim: BRG1 was required for hormone-induced changes in pioneer factor enrichment at GR peaks.
source: However, BRG1 was required for hormone-induced changes in pioneer factor enrichment at GR peaks.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data in BRG1-KD cells.

claim: In vehicle-treated cells, BRG1 peaks intersected 16.4% of FOXA1 peaks (1594 peaks) and 14.5% of GATA3 peaks (1145 peaks).
source: In vehicle-treated cells, BRG1 peaks intersected 16.4% of FOXA1 peaks (1594 peaks, Figure 6A,D) and 14.5% of GATA3 peaks (1145 peaks, Figure 6B,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 6A,B,D,E.

claim: Only 249 of the FOXA1 +BRG1 peaks intersected a GATA3 +BRG1 peak, similar to the overall proportion of overlap between FOXA1 and GATA3 peaks.
source: These peaks were predominantly unique, with only 249 of the FOXA1 +BRG1 peaks intersecting a GATA3 +BRG1 peak, similar to the overall proportion of overlap between FOXA1 and GATA3 peaks (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For both FOXA1 and GATA3, perfect GRE motifs were present at similar proportions between peaks with or without BRG1, with approximately 31% of FOXA1 peaks and 28% of GATA3 peaks having a perfect GRE motif within 500 bp of the center of the peak.
source: For both FOXA1 and GATA3, perfect GRE motifs were present at similar proportions between peaks with or without BRG1, with approximately 31% of FOXA1 peaks and 28% of GATA3 peaks having a perfect GRE motif within 500 bp of the center of the peak (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: GR binding at FOXA1 and GATA3 peaks was almost entirely restricted to peaks that intersected BRG1 peaks.
source: Despite this, GR binding at FOXA1 and GATA3 peaks was almost entirely restricted to peaks that intersected BRG1 peaks (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: ATAC-seq nucleosome-free reads and K27ac ChIP-seq signal were also predominantly restricted to pioneer factor peaks that intersected BRG1.
source: ATAC-seq nucleosome-free reads and K27ac ChIP-seq signal were also predominantly restricted to pioneer factor peaks that intersected BRG1 (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq and K27ac ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: The presence of BRG1 at pioneer factor peaks in untreated cells was predictive of subsequent GR binding upon Dex treatment.
source: Thus, the presence of BRG1 at pioneer factor peaks in untreated cells was predictive of subsequent GR binding upon Dex treatment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the correlation between BRG1 presence at pioneer factor peaks and subsequent GR binding.

claim: BRG1 is involved in pre-patterning a subset of pioneer factor binding sites to facilitate GR binding upon hormone treatment.
source: These findings suggest that BRG1 is involved in pre-patterning a subset of pioneer factor binding sites to facilitate GR binding upon hormone treatment and that pioneer factor binding alone is not predictive of GR binding.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the analysis of BRG1, pioneer factor, and GR binding patterns.

claim: Pioneer factor binding alone is not predictive of GR binding.
source: These findings suggest that BRG1 is involved in pre-patterning a subset of pioneer factor binding sites to facilitate GR binding upon hormone treatment and that pioneer factor binding alone is not predictive of GR binding.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the analysis of BRG1, pioneer factor, and GR binding patterns.

claim: Class II GR peaks represent GR binding to regions of chromatin that are pre-patterned by BRG1 and pioneer factors.
source: Class II GR peaks represent GR binding to regions of chromatin that are pre-patterned by BRG1 and pioneer factors.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined analysis of BRG1, pioneer factor, and GR binding patterns.

claim: BRG1 interacts with approximately 40% of GR binding sites prior to hormone treatment, and an additional 20% of GR binding sites upon hormone treatment.
source: Our data reveals that BRG1 interacts with approximately 40% of GR binding sites prior to hormone treatment, and an additional 20% of GR binding sites upon hormone treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis showing BRG1 binding at GR sites.

claim: BRG1 is broadly associated with transcriptional activity at active gene and enhancer TSSs.
source: BRG1 is also broadly associated with transcriptional activity at active gene and enhancer TSSs.
evidence: The claim is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data at TSSs.

claim: GR bound enhancers exist in three distinct chromatin states in mouse mammary adenocarcinoma cells.
source: These findings are corroborated by the observation that GR bound enhancers exist in three distinct chromatin states in mouse mammary adenocarcinoma cells (Johnson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study.

claim: Class I and Class III peaks gain chromatin accessibility upon Dex exposure and are associated with Dex-specific enhancer TSSs, suggesting that they represent regulatory elements that are activated only upon hormone treatment.
source: Class I and Class III peaks gain chromatin accessibility upon Dex exposure and are associated with Dex-specific enhancer TSSs, suggesting that they represent regulatory elements that are activated only upon hormone treatment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on ATAC-seq and Start-seq data.

claim: Class II GR binding sites are strikingly enriched for chromatin that is active and accessible prior to hormone signaling and appear to represent GR binding to active enhancers.
source: Class II GR binding sites are strikingly enriched for chromatin that is active and accessible prior to hormone signaling and appear to represent GR binding to active enhancers.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on ATAC-seq, histone modification, and transcriptional activity data.

claim: The majority of GR binding sites are not associated with transcriptional activity, indicating that GR binding to chromatin is not sufficient to activate transcription.
source: The majority of GR binding sites are not associated with transcriptional activity, indicating that GR binding to chromatin is not sufficient to activate transcription.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the comparison of GR binding sites and transcriptional activity.

claim: Active and accessible chromatin was only detected at Class II GR peaks where BRG1 localization was constitutive/hormone-independent.
source: Active and accessible chromatin was only detected at Class II GR peaks where BRG1 localization was constitutive/hormone-independent.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq and histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: This active chromatin environment was pre-existing, and was largely unchanged by Dex exposure and GR binding.
source: This active chromatin environment was pre-existing, and was largely unchanged by Dex exposure and GR binding.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on ATAC-seq and histone modification ChIP-seq data comparing EtOH and Dex conditions.

claim: BRG1 binding was not sufficient to generate a fully activated chromatin environment at GR binding sites, as Dex-induced recruitment of BRG1 at Class III peaks occurs without a concomitant induction of K27ac.
source: Furthermore, BRG1 binding was also not sufficient to generate a fully activated chromatin environment at GR binding sites, as Dex-induced recruitment of BRG1 at Class III peaks occurs without a concomitant induction of K27ac.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the comparison of BRG1 and K27ac ChIP-seq data at Class III peaks.

claim: A large subset of GR chromatin interactions are transcriptionally unproductive and uneventful in terms of the effect on the chromatin environment.
source: Thus, it appears that a large subset of GR chromatin interactions are transcriptionally unproductive and uneventful in terms of the effect on the chromatin environment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the lack of transcriptional activity and chromatin changes at many GR binding sites.

claim: Start-seq reveals that transcriptional activity is gained at ~25% of Class I peaks and ~30% of Class III peaks upon Dex exposure.
source: Despite this, Start-seq reveals that transcriptional activity is gained at ~25% of Class I peaks and ~30% of Class III peaks upon Dex exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by Start-seq data analysis.

claim: The induction of transcriptional activity at GR binding sites occurs independently of the induction of common active chromatin characteristics.
source: This suggests that the induction of transcriptional activity at GR binding sites occurs independently of the induction of common active chromatin characteristics.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the observation that transcriptional activity is gained without corresponding changes in chromatin marks.

claim: ~60% of Dex-regulated DEGs are lost following BRG1 knockdown, and Class II and III GR binding sites represent ~60% of GR binding sites.
source: Intriguingly, ~60% of Dex-regulated DEGs are lost following BRG1 knockdown, and Class II and III GR binding sites represent ~60% of GR binding sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in BRG1-KD cells and ChIP-seq data showing GR peak class proportions.

claim: The suppression of the GR transcriptional response following BRG1 knockdown suggested that BRG1 interaction with GR binding sites is required for GR-mediated transcriptional regulation of many genes.
source: The suppression of the GR transcriptional response following BRG1 knockdown suggested that BRG1 interaction with GR binding sites is required for GR-mediated transcriptional regulation of many genes.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on RNA-seq data in BRG1-KD cells.

claim: Over 100 genes gained hormone-responsiveness following BRG1 knockdown, indicating that at some genes, BRG1 prevents GR from eliciting transcriptional activity.
source: Surprisingly, over 100 genes gained hormone-responsiveness following BRG1 knockdown, indicating that at some genes, BRG1 prevents GR from eliciting transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in BRG1-KD cells showing 'gained' DEGs.

claim: BRG1 plays a critical role in patterning the GR transcriptional response.
source: Thus, BRG1 plays a critical role in patterning the GR transcriptional response.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the RNA-seq data in BRG1-KD cells showing both lost and gained DEGs.

claim: The distal nature of GR binding events and the enhancer-like characteristics of the chromatin under GR binding sites indicate that the GR signaling largely regulates transcription through modulation of enhancer activity.
source: The distal nature of GR binding events and the enhancer-like characteristics of the chromatin under GR binding sites indicate that the GR signaling largely regulates transcription through modulation of enhancer activity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the distance of GR binding from gene TSSs and the chromatin characteristics at GR binding sites.

claim: BRG1 was enriched at most active gene and enhancer TSSs, implicating a widespread role for BRG1 in facilitating transcriptional activity.
source: On the other hand, BRG1 was enriched at most active gene and enhancer TSSs, implicating a widespread role for BRG1 in facilitating transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on BRG1 ChIP-seq data at TSSs.

claim: Long-range chromatin interactions have been implicated in GR transcriptional activity.
source: Long-range chromatin interactions have been implicated in GR transcriptional activity (Vockley et al., 2016; Hakim et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies.

claim: It has been suggested that clusters of GBSs interact with each other over long ranges to synergistically regulate transcription of target genes.
source: It has also been suggested that clusters of GBSs interact with each other over long ranges to synergistically regulate transcription of target genes Holmqvist et al., 2005; Vockley et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies.

claim: GR and BRG1 could regulate gene expression through decompaction of broad regions of chromatin surrounding gene TSSs and enhancers, such as has been reported at the Fkbp5 and Ms4xxx loci in macrophages.
source: Alternatively, GR and BRG1 could regulate gene expression through decompaction of broad regions of chromatin surrounding gene TSSs and enhancers, such as has been reported at the Fkbp5 and Ms4xxx loci in macrophages (Jubb et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis supported by a cited study.

claim: BRG1 binding at Class II binding sites is predictive of potential GR interactions with pioneer factor binding sites.
source: We observed that BRG1 binding at Class II binding sites is predictive of potential GR interactions with pioneer factor binding sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of BRG1, GR, and pioneer factor ChIP-seq data.

claim: FOXA1 binding is reorganized upon activation of ER or GR.
source: This finding is intriguing when considered along with the recent finding that FOXA1 binding is reorganized upon activation of ER or GR (Swinstead et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study.

claim: BRG1 binding is significantly reorganized upon hormone treatment and the majority of EtOH-specific and Dex-specific BRG1 peaks are not associated with GR binding sites.
source: Like FOXA1, BRG1 binding is significantly reorganized upon hormone treatment and the majority of EtOH-specific and Dex-specific BRG1 peaks are not associated with GR binding sites [Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1].
evidence: The claim is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rearrangement of BRG1 and FOXA1 binding does not appear to be dependent on direct interaction with GR.
source: Thus, the rearrangement of BRG1 and FOXA1 binding does not appear to be dependent on direct interaction with GR.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the observation that many BRG1 and FOXA1 binding changes occur at sites without GR binding.

claim: The reorganization of BRG1 and FOXA1 binding may occur secondarily to the initial GR binding events, which occur rapidly within the first several minutes of hormone treatment.
source: While these rearrangements occur within an hour of hormone treatment, it is possible that the reorganization of BRG1 and FOXA1 binding occurs secondarily to the initial GR binding events, which occur rapidly within the first several minutes of hormone treatment (unpublished data).
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on unpublished data.

claim: It is possible that a subset of interactions between GR, BRG1 and FOXA1 on chromatin are not detectable by standard ChIP methods.
source: Alternatively, it is also possible that a subset of interactions between GR, BRG1 and FOXA1 on chromatin are not detectable by standard ChIP methods.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Single molecule analysis of GR, BRG1, and FOXA1 indicated that the majority of chromatin interactions occur with residence times of approximately 1 s, and a minority of events occur with longer residence times of 5 to 10 s.
source: Single molecule analysis of GR, BRG1, and FOXA1 indicated that the majority of chromatin interactions occur with residence times of approximately 1 s, and a minority of events occur with longer residence times of 5 to 10 s (Swinstead et al., 2016; Paakinaho et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies.

claim: Chromatin binding by GR, BRG1, and FOXA1 in individual cells is highly dynamic.
source: Thus, chromatin binding by these factors in individual cells is highly dynamic.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the cited single molecule analysis studies.

claim: ChIP-seq experiments could fail to detect the full expanse of rapid and dynamic binding events of GR, BRG1, and FOXA1.
source: While ChIP-seq experiments represent the overall binding profile of these factors in large populations of cells, they still represent snapshots of the chromatin interaction profiles of these factors and could fail to detect the full expanse of rapid and dynamic binding events.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on the limitations of ChIP-seq methodology.

claim: It remains unclear whether there is any set hierarchy of binding or timing/order of events of FOXA1, BRG1, and GR chromatin interactions.
source: As such, it remains unclear whether there is any set hierarchy of binding or timing/order of events of FOXA1, BRG1, and GR chromatin interactions.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of uncertainty based on the current data.

claim: It is likely that several series of binding events occur at GR binding sites prior to and upon hormone signaling.
source: As suggested by the distinct patterns of interactions at GR peak classes, it is likely that several series of binding events occur at GR binding sites prior to and upon hormone signaling.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed distinct patterns at different GR peak classes.

claim: The requirement for BRG1-mediated chromatin remodeling in potentiating the transcriptional response to glucocorticoid signaling at model genes (e.g. MMTV) was established over two decades ago.
source: The requirement for BRG1-mediated chromatin remodeling in potentiating the transcriptional response to glucocorticoid signaling at model genes (e.g. MMTV) was established over two decades ago.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge from prior research.

claim: GR preferentially binds to regions in the chromatin that are pre-accessible as measured by DNase hypersensitivity or formaldehyde-assisted isolation of regulatory elements.
source: GR preferentially binds to regions in the chromatin that are pre-accessible as measured by DNase hypersensitivity or formaldehyde-assisted isolation of regulatory elements (John et al., 2011; Burd et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies.

claim: GR chromatin interactions were predetermined by other chromatin interacting factors.
source: These findings indicated that GR chromatin interactions were predetermined by other chromatin interacting factors.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the observation that GR binds to pre-accessible chromatin.

claim: The pioneer factors C/EBPβ and AP1 pre-occupied a large proportion of GR binding sites in mouse liver and mammary cells, and were required to maintain chromatin accessibility at GR binding sites.
source: The pioneer factors C/EBPβ and AP1 pre-occupied a large proportion of GR binding sites in mouse liver and mammary cells, and were required to maintain chromatin accessibility at GR binding sites (Biddie et al., 2011; Grøntved et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies.

claim: FOXA1 pre-bound a large number of Estrogen Receptor (ER) binding sites and was required for ER binding and transcriptional activity.
source: Similarly, FOXA1 pre-bound a large number of Estrogen Receptor (ER, another nuclear hormone receptor closely related to GR) binding sites and was required for ER binding and transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge from prior research.

claim: Recent work has demonstrated that hormone signaling through both ER and GR promoted the redistribution of FOXA1 chromatin interactions.
source: Conversely, recent work has demonstrated that hormone signaling through both ER and GR promoted the redistribution of FOXA1 chromatin interactions (Swinstead et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study.

claim: Current models of GR activity fail to fully account for the complexities of GR signaling at a genomic scale.
source: These findings helped to demonstrate that current models of GR activity fail to fully account for the complexities of GR signaling at a genomic scale, and that more sophisticated and diverse models are required to describe the mechanisms through which GR initiates a transcriptional response.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the cited findings and the complexity of GR signaling.

claim: More sophisticated and diverse models are required to describe the mechanisms through which GR initiates a transcriptional response.
source: These findings helped to demonstrate that current models of GR activity fail to fully account for the complexities of GR signaling at a genomic scale, and that more sophisticated and diverse models are required to describe the mechanisms through which GR initiates a transcriptional response.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the complexity of GR signaling observed in the study.

claim: The Glucocorticoid Receptor (GR) alters transcriptional activity in response to hormones by interacting with chromatin at GR binding sites (GBSs) throughout the genome.
source: The Glucocorticoid Receptor (GR) alters transcriptional activity in response to hormones by interacting with chromatin at GR binding sites (GBSs) throughout the genome.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about GR function.

claim: BRG1 interacts with GBSs prior to hormone exposure.
source: Our work in human breast cancer cells identifies three classes of GBSs with distinct epigenetic characteristics and reveals that BRG1 interacts with GBSs prior to hormone exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing BRG1 binding at GR sites before hormone treatment.

claim: The GBSs pre-occupied by BRG1 are more accessible and transcriptionally active than other GBSs.
source: The GBSs pre-occupied by BRG1 are more accessible and transcriptionally active than other GBSs.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq and transcriptional activity data comparing different GR peak classes.

claim: BRG1 is required for a proper and robust transcriptional hormone response.
source: BRG1 is required for a proper and robust transcriptional hormone response and knockdown of BRG1 blocks recruitment of the pioneer factors FOXA1 and GATA3 to GBSs.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in BRG1-KD cells showing loss of hormone-responsive genes.

claim: Knockdown of BRG1 blocks recruitment of the pioneer factors FOXA1 and GATA3 to GBSs.
source: BRG1 is required for a proper and robust transcriptional hormone response and knockdown of BRG1 blocks recruitment of the pioneer factors FOXA1 and GATA3 to GBSs.
evidence: The claim is supported by FOXA1 and GATA3 ChIP-seq data in BRG1-KD cells.

claim: GR interaction with FOXA1 and GATA3 binding sites was restricted to sites pre-bound by BRG1.
source: Finally, GR interaction with FOXA1 and GATA3 binding sites was restricted to sites pre-bound by BRG1.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing GR binding at pioneer factor sites only when BRG1 is present.

claim: BRG1 establishes specialized chromatin environments that define multiple classes of GBS.
source: These findings demonstrate that BRG1 establishes specialized chromatin environments that define multiple classes of GBS.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined analysis of BRG1 binding, chromatin accessibility, and histone modifications at different GR peak classes.

claim: GR and other transcriptional activators function via multiple distinct chromatin-based mechanisms to modulate the transcriptional response.
source: This in turn predicts that GR and other transcriptional activators function via multiple distinct chromatin-based mechanisms to modulate the transcriptional response.
evidence: The claim is a speculative prediction based on the observation of distinct GR peak classes with different chromatin characteristics.
